name: Boeing 737 Next Generation
summary: Third-generation 737, still the most common airliner in the US with Southwest, United, American, Delta and Alaska; the military flies it as the C-40 Clipper.

wings: Low swept wing that looks long for the fuselage
Tall curved blended winglets, split-scimitar winglets (big curved upper blade plus small lower strake), or plain tips
engines: Two CFM56-7B engines in nacelles with a flattened bottom ('hamster pouch' intake)
Engines mounted very close under and ahead of the wing
Plain, smooth nacelle trailing edge — no chevrons
fuselage: Narrow, pointed nose with V-notched cockpit side windows
Short landing gear — sits low to the ground
Main wheels have no outer doors; hubcaps are visible in the belly in flight
tail: Long dorsal fillet sweeping up into the fin
Tailcone ending in a short pointed vertical wedge

tellTales: Flat-bottomed engine intakes tucked tight under the wing
Exposed main-wheel hubcaps in the belly
Pointed nose with a long dorsal fillet into the fin

confusedWith.howToTell: The NG has smooth nacelle exhausts, flat-bottomed intakes and blended or scimitar winglets; the MAX has sawtooth chevron exhausts, rounder bigger engines and a twin-blade 'AT' winglet.
The 737NG has a pointed nose with V-notched side windows, shorter gear and exposed wheel hubs; the A320 has a blunt rounded nose and covered main wheels.
The P-8 is a grey 737-800 airframe with raked wingtips instead of winglets, few cabin windows and a weapons bay and sensor fairings under the fuselage.
The 737NG has short gear and a shorter body; the 757 is far longer and stands on tall gear with much larger engines.

usCount.source: Airline fleet data (Southwest, United, American, Delta, Alaska; planespotters.net) plus ~30 C-40A/B/C (USN, USMC, USAF fact sheets)
